task_title: Aircraft Systems Related to Instrument Flight Rules (IFR) Operations
objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how your airplane's ice protection, pitot-static, vacuum, electrical, flight control and autopilot systems work, what their limits are, and what to do when ice builds or a system fails in instrument conditions.
why: In the clouds you can't see ice building or a gyro slowly dying. Pilots who know their systems and their limits catch the problem early and get out before it turns into a loss of control.

prereading.what: Deicing and anti-icing systems, propeller, antenna and pitot-static icing, icing certification, airplanes not certificated for icing, ice detection and SLD cues.
prereading.label: AC 91-74B Ch 3, pp 19-30

prereading.what: Icing rules, talking to ATC, preflight, takeoff, cruise, autopilot use, holding, approach and landing, wing stall, tailplane stall and roll upsets.
prereading.label: AC 91-74B Ch 5, pp 39-49

prereading.label: IFH Ch 4, 4-13 to 4-17

prereading.what: The heated pitot-static system, blocked pitot and static errors, and the alternate static source.
prereading.label: IFH Ch 5, 5-2 to 5-3

prereading.what: Inadvertent icing encounter, alternator failure, standby battery, analog and vacuum instrument failure, and pitot-static failure.
prereading.label: IFH Ch 11, 11-2 to 11-8

warmup: Your IFR trainer has a heated pitot tube and an alternate static source. Does that make it legal and safe to climb through a cloud layer at -4 °C? What would you need to find out first?

key_terms.def: Turned on before ice forms, to keep a surface completely free of ice.
Used after ice forms. It lets some ice build, then breaks it off, like pneumatic boots.
Conditions where ice is actually seen or detected forming on the airplane in flight.
Liquid drops bigger than 0.05 mm below 0 °C: freezing drizzle or freezing rain.
Ice left on, or built up between, deicing cycles. A deiced wing is never fully clean.
Water that runs back off a protected area and freezes on an unprotected surface.
Ice-contaminated tailplane stall: an iced tail stalls, often after full flaps, and the nose pitches down.
A small part you can see from the seat, like a wiper or strut, that ices first and warns you.
Backup static air, usually from the cabin, for when the outside static ports are blocked.
Shows the vacuum that spins the air-driven attitude and heading gyros.
Power bus a standby battery keeps alive after a charging failure: AHRS, ADC, PFD, one nav and one com.
Automatic flight control system: servos move the controls to hold attitude, heading, altitude or a course.

chunks.title: Icing: where ice forms and what it does

body.p: Structural ice forms when supercooled water droplets hit the airplane and freeze. Small, thin parts collect ice fastest. The tail is a better collector than the wing because it is thinner [[23:90|IFH 4-13]].

Expect icing whenever you fly in visible moisture, like cloud or rain, and the temperature is between +02 and -10 °C [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]]. Ice usually builds fastest not far below 0 °C. Below about -20 °C most clouds are ice crystals, which bounce off [[38:13|AC 91-74B 2-1]].

head: Ice type
What it looks like
Favored by
rows: Clear (glaze)
Glossy, clear, hard. Large amounts can form horns [[23:90|IFH 4-13]] [[23:91|IFH 4-14]]
Temperatures near freezing, lots of liquid water, high speed, large drops [[23:91|IFH 4-14]]
Rime
Rough, milky, opaque, brittle [[23:91|IFH 4-14]]
Low temperatures, less liquid water, low speed, small drops [[23:91|IFH 4-14]]
Mixed
Clear and rime together. The shape and roughness matter most [[23:91|IFH 4-14]]
Clear and rime forming on the same surface [[23:91|IFH 4-14]]

body.p: Ice changes the wing's shape. The wing stalls at a lower angle of attack and a higher airspeed. In cruise, at a low angle of attack, you may hardly notice it. Then you slow down for the approach and the stall comes early [[23:91|IFH 4-14]] [[23:92|IFH 4-15]].

bullets: A 30% loss of maximum lift is not unusual. Horn ice can cost 40% to 50% [[23:92|IFH 4-15]].
Drag can rise 100%, and 200% or more with horns [[23:92|IFH 4-15]].
A thin, rough layer can hurt more than a bigger smooth one [[38:11|AC 91-74B 1-4d]].
Ice effects add up: less thrust, more drag, less lift, more weight. In extreme cases 2 to 3 inches can form in under 5 minutes [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]].

callout.text: Without wing protection, the first sign is often lower airspeed or more power needed. With limited power, you may soon be near the stall [[38:23|AC 91-74B 3-3]].

check.q: Why can ice that barely changed anything in cruise suddenly matter on the approach?
check.a: Ice lowers the stall angle of attack. Slowing down raises the angle of attack, so the stall comes at a higher speed than normal [[23:91|IFH 4-14]] [[23:92|IFH 4-15]].

chunks.title: Anti-ice and deice: airframe ice protection

head: Anti-icing
Deicing
rows: Job
Keep a surface entirely free of ice [[38:25|AC 91-74B 3-5]]
Remove ice after some has built up [[38:23|AC 91-74B 3-4]]
When on
Before you enter icing. Using it as a deicer can damage it [[38:25|AC 91-74B 3-5]]
At the first sign of ice [[38:24|AC 91-74B 3-4a(2)]]
Examples
Heated pitot, heated static ports and fuel vents, windshield heat or alcohol, heated stall warning [[24:258|AFH 13-9]]; chemical "weeping" wings [[38:26|AC 91-74B 3-5b]]
Pneumatic boots, electroimpact, cycling electrothermal heat [[38:23|AC 91-74B 3-4]] [[38:24|AC 91-74B 3-4c]]

body.p: **Pneumatic boots** are rubber tubes on the wing and tail leading edges. Suction holds them flat. A timer inflates them to crack the ice, and the airflow blows it off [[38:23|AC 91-74B 3-4a]].

bullets: Ice builds between cycles, so a booted wing is never fully clean. It may take many cycles before ice sheds [[38:23|AC 91-74B 3-4a(1)]] [[38:24|AC 91-74B 3-4a(1)]].
Cycle early and often. Activating early never leaves more ice on the wing than waiting [[38:24|AC 91-74B 3-4a(2)]].
Ice bridging has few, if any, documented cases on modern boots [[38:24|AC 91-74B 3-4a(4)]].
Keep cycling for a while after you leave the ice so the wing is as clean as possible for landing [[38:24|AC 91-74B 3-4a(3)]].
Boots crack with age, and pinholes draw in moisture that can freeze. Inspect them [[38:33|AC 91-74B 3-14]].

body.p: **Chemical (weeping) systems** spread a fluid such as isopropyl alcohol or ethylene glycol that lowers the freezing point. They are used on some piston airplanes too [[38:26|AC 91-74B 3-5b]]. Fluid systems can take several minutes to prime, so check for fluid along the whole leading edge [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-4b(4)]].

callout.text: ANTI = before (prevent). DE = after (remove). Rule of thumb: anti-ice at the first visible moisture when the air is a little above freezing or colder; deice at the first sign of ice [[38:59|AC 91-74B App 2]] [[38:26|AC 91-74B 3-5b]].

check.q: Your POH does not say otherwise. When do you first cycle the boots?
check.a: At the first sign of ice. The FAA recommends early activation; it never leaves more ice than waiting [[38:24|AC 91-74B 3-4a(2)]].

chunks.title: Propeller, engine intake, fuel and other systems

body.p: Every airplane must have ice protection for its engine in case of an inadvertent encounter. Nearly all have pitot heat and an alternate static source [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13a]]. Here is what else can ice up.

head: System
What ice does
Protection
rows: Propeller

Less thrust. Most ice collects on the spinner and inner blade [[23:93|IFH 4-16]]. In one SLD test, ice on the whole blade cost 50 knots in 1 minute 25 seconds, with no rpm change on a constant-speed prop [[38:28|AC 91-74B 3-8]]
Electrically heated boots, heated in balanced sections [[38:25|AC 91-74B 3-4c(1)]]
Carburetor
Ice in the venturi chokes the engine, from 20 °F to 70 °F (-7 °C to 21 °C) [[23:90|IFH 4-13]]
Carburetor heat is an anti-icing system; use it to prevent ice [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]
Air intake
Impact ice blocks the inlet: rpm drops (fixed pitch) or manifold pressure drops (constant speed) [[24:258|AFH 13-9]]
Carb heat or alternate air; some open automatically [[24:258|AFH 13-9]] [[1:171|PHAK 7-11]]
Fuel
Water in fuel freezes into crystals that block screens, strainers and filters [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]]
Drain sumps every preflight; approved additives on some airplanes [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]]. Heated or non-icing fuel vents [[24:258|AFH 13-9]]
Windshield
You can't see out [[38:30|AC 91-74B 3-11d]]
Heated plate or fluid spray bar [[38:30|AC 91-74B 3-11d]]. No system? Defroster on high [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-5d]]
Antennas
Ice makes them vibrate or "howl", distorts signals, or breaks them off [[38:28|AC 91-74B 3-9]]
Usually none. Carry a handheld radio [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(6)]]
Stall warning
The vane or switch can freeze. Even if it works, the iced wing stalls before it warns [[38:29|AC 91-74B 3-11c]]
Heated vane on some airplanes [[38:29|AC 91-74B 3-11c(1)]]

callout.text: Carburetor heat can also serve as alternate air if the intake filter clogs in sudden airframe icing [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]]. Fuel additives never replace carburetor heat [[1:188|PHAK 7-28]].

check.q: You fly a constant-speed prop. Prop ice is building. Why may the tachometer not warn you?
check.a: The governor flattens the blade pitch to hold rpm, so you see no rpm change while airspeed falls [[38:28|AC 91-74B 3-8]].

chunks.title: Pitot heat, static ports and the alternate static source

body.p: The airspeed indicator uses pitot and static pressure. The altimeter and VSI use static pressure only [[23:97|IFH 5-2]]. Even light icing can block the pitot entry hole, which is why most airplanes have pitot heat [[38:28|AC 91-74B 3-11a]]. Static port areas may also be heated [[23:97|IFH 5-2]].

head: Blockage
Airspeed
Altimeter and VSI
rows: Pitot hole blocked, drain open
Slowly drops to zero [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Normal
Pitot hole and drain blocked
Acts like an altimeter: rises in a climb, falls in a descent [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Normal
Static port blocked
Above the blockage altitude, reads low. Below it, reads high [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Altimeter freezes; VSI stays at zero [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Alternate static (cabin air) selected
Reads higher than actual [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Altimeter reads slightly high; VSI shows a brief climb [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]

body.p: The alternate source usually opens to the cabin, where pressure is lower because of the airflow around the fuselage [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. The POH often has a correction table for it [[24:258|AFH 13-9]]. With no alternate source in an unpressurized airplane, you could break the VSI glass to give the altimeter and airspeed static air. Expect more errors [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

A **partial** static blockage is sneaky. It may show nothing until you descend. Then you look too high and too fast, descending slower than you are [[24:363|AFH 18-14]] [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. To check, open the alternate static while climbing or descending. If the needles jump, keep it on for the rest of the flight [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

callout.text: Glass panels: the backup instruments often share the same pitot and static lines, so both can fail together. Where ADC and AHRS are combined, a blockage may even affect attitude [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

check.q: In cruise, the airspeed slowly unwinds to zero while altitude and VSI look normal. Likely cause and first fix?
check.a: Iced pitot tube with the drain hole open [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. Make sure pitot heat is on; that is what it is for [[38:28|AC 91-74B 3-11a]].

chunks.title: Approved for ice? Certification and the rules

body.p: An airplane certificated for IFR is not necessarily certificated for flight in icing conditions. Only the AFM or POH tells you [[38:10|AC 91-74B 1-4a]]. Ice protection equipment, even a lot of it, does not by itself mean approval [[24:258|AFH 13-9]].

callout.text: 14 CFR 91.527 (icing) sits in Part 91 subpart F, which covers only large airplanes, turbojet multiengine airplanes and fractional ownership aircraft [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501(a)]] [[60:536|14 CFR 91.527]]. For a typical single-engine trainer there is no specific icing rule, but 91.9 bans flying outside the AFM limitations and placards [[38:43|AC 91-74B 5-2]] [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(a)]]. Careless or reckless operation is banned too [[60:436|14 CFR 91.13(a)]].

body.p: **How to tell if a small airplane is approved** [[38:31|AC 91-74B 3-12c]]:

bullets: The AFM or POH refers to "part 25 appendix C" icing conditions, or to 14 CFR 23.1419 at Amendment 23-14 or later.
The Type Certificate Data Sheet certification basis lists 23.1419 at Amendment 23-14 or higher, or SFAR 23.
If the AFM only has an equipment list for icing, the basis is older than Amendment 23-14 (1973).

head: Built or certified
What it means for you
rows: Before 1973
No icing tests. Treat the ice protection as a way to exit [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-12d(4)]]
Below Amendment 23-43
Do not rely on the stall warning in ice [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-12d]]
Icing-certified after 1994
Tested for tailplane stall. Follow the AFM flap limits [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-12d(3)]]
Not certified, but has boots ("non-hazard")
Emergency use only. Performance unknown, stall warning likely won't work, controls may jam [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13c]] [[38:33|AC 91-74B 3-13c(2)]]

body.p: Even an approved airplane has limits. Certification does not cover freezing drizzle or freezing rain, and some airplanes are banned from them [[38:43|AC 91-74B 5-2a]]. SLD can put ice behind the protected areas [[38:31|AC 91-74B 3-12b]]. Some STC equipment can affect the icing approval [[38:31|AC 91-74B 3-12b]].

head: Intensity (AIM)
Meaning
Your move
rows: Trace
Noticeable; under 1/4 inch per hour
Consider exiting before it gets worse [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]]
Light
Occasional cycling of manual deice; 1/4 to 1 inch per hour
Consider exiting [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]]
Moderate
Frequent cycling; 1 to 3 inches per hour
Consider exiting as soon as possible [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]]
Severe
Protection can't keep up; ice aft of protected areas
Immediate exit [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]]

check.q: Your trainer is IFR certified and has pitot heat. Where do you look to see if it may fly into known icing?
check.a: The AFM or POH (limitations, and whether it cites part 25 appendix C or 23.1419), or the TCDS. IFR approval is not icing approval [[38:10|AC 91-74B 1-4a]] [[38:31|AC 91-74B 3-12c]].

body.p: Small airplanes mostly use mechanical controls: rods, cables and pulleys carry your inputs to the surfaces [[1:149|PHAK 6-1]]. Big, fast airplanes may use boosted or fly-by-wire controls, where the feel is simulated [[1:150|PHAK 6-2]].

head: Group
Parts
Job
rows: Primary
Ailerons, elevator (or stabilator), rudder
Needed to control the airplane safely [[1:150|PHAK 6-2]]
Secondary
Flaps, leading edge devices, spoilers, trim
Improve performance or remove control pressure [[1:150|PHAK 6-2]]

body.p: Trim tabs move opposite to the elevator. Full nose-down trim moves the tab up [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]]. Set power, pitch and configuration first, then trim off the pressure. Retrim after every change [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]] [[1:159|PHAK 6-11]]. Good trim matters in IFR: poor trim can turn a short distraction into an emergency if you stop cross-checking [[23:219|IFH 7-58]].

head: Failure
What to do
rows: Up-elevator cable breaks
Lots of nose-up trim, then use forward pressure to control pitch [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Down-elevator cable breaks
Lots of nose-down trim, then use back pressure [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Elevator linkage fails
Trim tab can still raise or lower the elevator, usually enough to land [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Flaps won't extend
No-flap landing; may need up to 50% more runway [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Split flap
Roll toward the less-flapped wing; opposite aileron and rudder, fly faster [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]

callout.text: Ice can partly block control surfaces or make them ineffective [[23:92|IFH 4-15]]. Ice ahead of the ailerons can cause "aileron snatch", a sudden change in control force [[38:26|AC 91-74B 3-6b(2)]].

check.q: You have to hold steady back pressure on the yoke. What should you do?
check.a: Add nose-up trim until the pressure is gone [[1:158|PHAK 6-10]].

chunks.title: Ice on the controls: tailplane stall and roll upset

body.p: The tail pushes down to balance the nose-heavy wing. Flaps and higher speed make the tail's angle more negative. With ice on the tail, it can stall when you lower flaps, and the nose drops [[23:92|IFH 4-15]] [[38:26|AC 91-74B 3-7a]]. You usually can't see the tail to check it [[23:92|IFH 4-15]].

head: Wing stall
Tailplane stall (ICTS)
rows: Usually when
Any phase [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10e]]; most icing accidents are wing stalls [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12b]]
Rarely before full flaps [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10e]]; none known in cruise [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12a]]
Signs
Buffet or shudder: treat it as an imminent stall [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-7a]]. Certified for ice before 2000? You may get only buffet, no stall warning [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12b]]
Elevator pulsing, odd nose-down trim change, loss of elevator effect, sudden nose-down pitch [[23:93|IFH 4-16]]
Recovery
Normal stall recovery from the FAA template or AFM: reduce the angle of attack [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-11c]] [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-13a]]
Flaps back to the previous setting, nose-up elevator, only the speed that flap setting needs, power per the maker, slow nose-down changes, cycle the boots [[23:93|IFH 4-16]]
More speed
Moves the wing away from a stall [[23:92|IFH 4-15]]
At the same flap setting, makes it worse. More power may too, in some designs [[23:93|IFH 4-16]] [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-12d]]

body.p: Suspect a wing stall with any buffet unless you just lowered full flaps [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12b]]. Lower speed moves you toward a wing stall; higher speed toward a tail stall, so the safe window is small [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12c]] [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-12c]].

**Roll upset** is an uncommanded roll from ice ahead of the ailerons, often in SLD [[23:92|IFH 4-15]] [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-13]]. Reduce pitch to lower the angle of attack, roll wings level, set power and watch airspeed. Don't retract flaps unless the wing top is clear of ice [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-13a]].

callout.text: Roll upset and wing stall recovery are partly the opposite of tailplane stall recovery. Using the wrong one makes it worse [[38:53|AC 91-74B 5-13]].

check.q: You lower full flaps on short final after flying in ice. The yoke goes light and the nose pitches down. What do you do?
check.a: Suspect a tailplane stall: retract the flaps to the previous setting, apply nose-up elevator, use only the airspeed that flap setting needs, set power per the maker, and make nose-down changes slowly [[23:93|IFH 4-16]].

chunks.title: The vacuum system and gyro failure

body.p: IFR requires an attitude indicator, a heading indicator and a rate-of-turn indicator [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)]]. Makers power them from different sources, so one failure doesn't take them all. Many airplanes use air-driven attitude and heading gyros with an electric turn coordinator [[23:112|IFH 5-17]].

bullets: An engine-driven pump sucks air through the gyro cases. A suction-relief valve holds the right vacuum, shown on the suction gauge [[23:112|IFH 5-17]].
A typical run-up reading is 4.8 to 5.2 inches of mercury at 2,000 rpm. Use your POH value [[24:59|AFH 2-22]].
On some airplanes the same pump inflates the deice boots [[23:112|IFH 5-17]], and suction holds the boots flat [[38:23|AC 91-74B 3-4a]].
Older venturi systems can clog with ice and stop the gyros when you need them most [[23:112|IFH 5-17]].

body.p: When the pump fails, the gyros slow down and wander. If they feed the autopilot or flight director, those can move the wrong way too [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. In the picture the airplane is level at 2,000 ft, not turning left. A pilot who misses the OFF flags may turn a calm problem into a dangerous one [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

Many small airplanes have no vacuum warning, so scan the suction gauge [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Find the failure by comparing the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and VSI. Then fly on the instruments that work, try to restore the failed ones, and tell ATC [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

callout.text: Covering the failed instruments helps you ignore them [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]. Practice partial panel often [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

check.q: The attitude indicator shows a left bank, but the turn coordinator is level and altitude and VSI are steady. What failed?
check.a: Probably the vacuum system or attitude gyro. Rate and static instruments say level flight. Check the suction gauge and OFF flags [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

chunks.title: The electrical system and alternator failure

body.p: IFR requires a generator or alternator of adequate capacity [[60:488|14 CFR 91.205(d)(7)]]. Pitot heat is electric [[23:97|IFH 5-2]]. Many airplanes use electric turn indicators [[23:112|IFH 5-17]], and glass panels run the AHRS, air data computer and engine displays on it [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

bullets: Signs: an ammeter showing discharge (minus), the loadmeter (the alternator's load), or an alternator warning light [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].
Battery time is roughly 40 minutes, or 30 to 40 minutes of useful voltage, but don't count on it [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].
Never continue the flight. Land at the nearest suitable airport [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].
Shed load: duplicate radios, nonessential lights. Pull circuit breakers if you must [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].

body.p: In a glass-panel airplane, losing the alternator is an emergency, not just an abnormal [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. A standby battery comes online near 19 volts and powers the essential bus, but only if its switch is in ARM. Arm it before departure [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. When it runs out, you have the standby attitude, altimeter, airspeed and compass, and pilotage unless you carry a handheld GPS [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

head: Battery load (25 amp-hour battery)
About how long
rows: 5 amps
10 amps
Maybe 2 hours [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]
40 amps

callout.text: Electric flaps and gear draw big loads. On a weak battery they can cause an instant total power loss. Plan a no-flap landing and a manual gear extension [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].

Under IFR in controlled airspace, report any nav, approach or comm equipment malfunction to ATC as soon as practical [[60:483|14 CFR 91.187]]. Tell ATC about the coming electrical failure early [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

check.q: Why is an alternator failure a bigger deal in icing conditions?
check.a: Pitot heat is electric [[23:97|IFH 5-2]], and once the battery is gone you may lose it and much more. Shed load and land as soon as practical [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

chunks.title: Autopilots and automatic flight control systems

body.p: An autopilot is an automatic flight control system. Servos move the controls to hold the airplane level or on a course. The common modes are altitude hold and heading hold [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]].

head: Type
What it controls
rows: Single-axis
Roll only: one servo on the ailerons (a wing leveler) [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]]
Two-axis (most GA)
Roll and pitch [[23:120|IFH 5-25]]
Three-axis
Roll, pitch and yaw: aileron, elevator and rudder servos [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]]

body.p: Some autopilots sense attitude (position based). Others use a turn-and-bank sensor (rate based) [[23:120|IFH 5-25]]. Advanced ones add vertical speed or airspeed hold and couple to nav signals through a flight director [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]]. A flight director only shows steering commands; it does not mean the autopilot is flying [[23:119|IFH 5-24]].

Know which modes are **engaged** and which are **armed**, and check that armed modes engage when they should [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. In the picture, the display shows HDG and VS HLD (engaged: holding heading and a 400 fpm climb) and APR ARM (armed, waiting to capture). That VS climb is exactly the mode AC 91-74B says not to climb in when there is ice [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-6c]]. Watch for traps: on some systems, switching the nav source from GPS to LOC or VOR while in NAV mode drops the autopilot to ROL (wings level) until you reselect NAV [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

bullets: There is a disconnect that works automatically or manually, and you can overpower the autopilot [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]].
Systems differ a lot. Use the autopilot instructions in your AFM or POH [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]].
Read the avionics and autopilot manuals for your airplane [[1:68|PHAK 2-29]].

check.q: Your flight director bars are showing but the autopilot light is off. Who is flying?
check.a: You are. A flight director only gives steering commands for the pilot, or the autopilot if coupled, to follow [[23:119|IFH 5-24]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: ice protection on an IFR flight

body.p: **Planning**

bullets: 1. Open the POH: is the airplane approved for icing, what systems work, and what are the limits [[38:10|AC 91-74B 1-4a]]? Check the MEL or equipment list for what may be inoperative [[38:33|AC 91-74B 3-14b]].
2. Plan exits: can you climb or descend out of ice and still clear terrain and routes? Mark airports along the way [[38:45|AC 91-74B 5-4a]] [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(3)]].
3. Pick alternates with longer runways, take extra fuel, a bright flashlight and a handheld radio [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a]].

body.p: **Preflight and taxi**

bullets: 4. Remove all frost, snow and ice. Even a little hurts the wing [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(9)]].

5. Check the pitot cover is off and the static ports are clear [[23:131|IFH 5-36]]. Check deice fluid quantity, that the alternate static valve opens and is fully closed, and pitot heat by watching the ammeter [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].
6. After start, check suction or electrical sources for the gyros, then the deice and anti-ice systems [[23:132|IFH 5-37]]. Do the POH pretakeoff check of those systems [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-5]].
7. Check full control movement and carburetor heat. No windshield system? Defroster on high [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-5]].

body.p: **In flight**

bullets: 8. Before takeoff into cloud, confirm pitot heat ON and the airspeed alive [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-6a]].

9. In visible moisture, watch the OAT [[23:327|IFH 11-2]]. Anti-ice on at the first visible moisture when the temperature is a little above freezing or colder; deice at the first ice [[38:59|AC 91-74B App 2]].
10. Scan your ice evidence probe and the areas behind protected surfaces. Use a flashlight at night [[38:34|AC 91-74B 3-15b]] [[23:327|IFH 11-2]].
11. Set an airspeed bug, and if workload allows, hand-fly now and then to feel changes [[38:60|AC 91-74B App 2]].
12. Cycle the boots before final. Fly a higher approach speed, carry some power in the flare, and use a longer runway [[38:60|AC 91-74B App 2]].

callout.text: On the checkride, have your POH tabbed: kinds of operations limits, ice protection procedures, alternate static correction, and the autopilot supplement.

check.q: How does the IFH say to check the pitot heater on preflight?
check.a: Turn it on and watch the ammeter, or use the POH method [[23:132|IFH 5-37]].

chunks.title: Risk: operating in icing and the limits of ice protection

body.p: Not approved for icing? Avoid it, and exit at once if you meet it [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13b]]. Approved? The equipment gives you time to get out; it is not built for staying in ice forever [[23:327|IFH 11-2]].

**Getting out.** Leave the precipitation, or go to an altitude above freezing. That warmer altitude is not always lower [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]]. If neither works, consider landing at the nearest suitable airport [[23:327|IFH 11-2]].

**ATC.** Controllers don't know your equipment. Tell them how bad the ice is, what it is doing to the airplane, and what you need [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b]]. Not approved for ice? Declare an emergency [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b]]. Many pilots in icing accidents deviated without declaring, or turned down ATC's offer to declare one [[38:10|AC 91-74B 1-4b]].

head: Limit or number
Source
rows: Keep at least 1.5 to 1.6 × Vs (clean) in ice. Turn down ATC speeds below that
Airspeed has gone from cruise to stall in under 3 minutes
Can't hold airspeed with more power? Exit immediately
No AFM icing speed: approach at least 25% faster
Landing distance grows 20% for each 10% more speed
Freezing drizzle or rain: don't stay in it, even if approved

bullets: Change configuration with care. Ice that was harmless in cruise can bite with flaps [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7d]].
Holding is risky: slower and lower. Many AFMs limit flap use in ice [[38:50|AC 91-74B 5-9]].
Most icing accidents happen in the final phases of flight [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10d]].
SLD clues: ice behind the boots, jagged ice lines, granular ice on side windows, rain or drizzle below +5 °C. Ask for a new route or altitude [[38:34|AC 91-74B 3-16]].
No PIREPs doesn't mean no ice. A big jet's "light" can be a small airplane's "severe" [[38:40|AC 91-74B 4-3]].

callout.text: Under IFR in controlled airspace, report any unforecast weather you meet [[60:482|14 CFR 91.183(b)]]. An icing PIREP helps everyone behind you [[38:41|AC 91-74B 4-3b(4)]].

check.q: Clean stall speed is 60 knots. What is the minimum speed margin AC 91-74B suggests in icing?
check.a: At least 1.5 to 1.6 × Vs: 90 to 96 knots [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-7a]].

body.p: In single-pilot IFR, the autopilot cuts workload, frees you to manage the flight, and lowers the chance of an unusual attitude or CFIT [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]] [[23:219|IFH 7-58]]. But it can also hide trouble.

head: Hazard
What happens
What to do
rows: Masked ice
The autopilot hides handling changes. At disconnect you may need big forces; on unboosted controls it can trip off with the controls deflected [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7e]]
Hand-fly now and then, or watch for odd trim and attitude [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7f]]
Altitude hold
Without autothrottle it holds altitude while airspeed bleeds toward a stall [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7f]]
Watch airspeed. Add power at level-off [[38:50|AC 91-74B 5-8c]]
Vertical speed mode
In ice it holds the climb rate until the stall [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-6d]]
Don't climb in VS mode in ice. Prefer airspeed hold [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7f]]
Dying gyro
Wandering vacuum gyros can drive the autopilot the wrong way [[23:332|IFH 11-7]]
Cross-check, then disconnect
Mode confusion
A mode drops or never arms [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]
Say the modes out loud after each change [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]

body.p: People are poor at watching automation. The more reliable it is, the worse we get at catching its faults, and light workload breeds complacency [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. A malfunctioning or misused autopilot can cause an upset. Disconnecting it gives you direct control, so keep your hand-flying skills [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

bullets: Pick the level of automation that fits the workload; there is no one right level [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]] [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].
Autopilot inoperative before departure? Count it in your risk. Plan before takeoff how you will handle an autopilot failure [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].
An unexpected disconnect from ice is most dangerous low on the approach [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10c]].
In an inadvertent thunderstorm encounter, disengage altitude hold and speed hold; they only add structural stress [[23:327|IFH 11-2]].

check.q: You are climbing in ice with the autopilot in VS mode at 500 fpm. What is the danger?
check.a: As ice builds, the autopilot keeps the climb rate and lets airspeed decay until the stall [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-6d]].

bullets: Thinking an IFR airplane is approved for ice [[38:10|AC 91-74B 1-4a]].
Quoting 91.527 for a single-engine trainer instead of the AFM limits under 91.9 [[38:43|AC 91-74B 5-2]].
Waiting for ice to build before cycling boots [[38:24|AC 91-74B 3-4a(2)]].
Turning anti-ice on late and using it like a deicer [[38:25|AC 91-74B 3-5]].
Taking off into cloud with pitot heat off [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-6a]].
Trusting the stall warning with ice on the wing [[38:29|AC 91-74B 3-11c(2)]].
Lowering full flaps with ice on the tail [[38:27|AC 91-74B 3-7b]].
Climbing in VS mode, or letting altitude hold bleed off airspeed [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-6c]] [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7f]].
Missing the OFF flags and not scanning the suction gauge [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].
Continuing after an alternator failure or running electric flaps on a weak battery [[23:330|IFH 11-5]] [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].
Deviating for ice without telling ATC or declaring an emergency [[38:10|AC 91-74B 1-4b]].

check.q: Why is a stall warning horn not enough protection in icing?
check.a: The iced wing stalls at a lower angle of attack, so the stall can come before the warning [[38:29|AC 91-74B 3-11c(2)]].

scenario.title: Rime on the climb, a busy frequency and an autopilot in VS mode
scenario.setup: You depart IFR in a single-engine piston airplane that is not approved for flight in icing. It has pitot heat, an alternate static source and a two-axis autopilot. The forecast showed tops at 7,000 ft and a freezing level at 4,000 ft. You are climbing to 8,000 ft with the autopilot in vertical speed mode at 500 fpm. Passing 5,500 ft, OAT -3 °C, you see rime building on the wing strut and windshield edge. The airspeed is 12 knots below your normal climb speed and dropping. The frequency is very busy.

questions.q: What is the autopilot doing to you right now?
questions.a: In VS mode it holds 500 fpm while ice adds drag, so airspeed keeps falling and it will hold the rate until the stall [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-6d]]. Disconnect or change mode and fly airspeed; airspeed hold is the preferred vertical mode [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7f]].

questions.q: Is it legal or wise to keep climbing to the tops?
questions.a: This airplane is not approved for icing, so you must avoid ice and exit at once [[38:32|AC 91-74B 3-13b]]. Its AFM limits bind you under 91.9 [[38:43|AC 91-74B 5-2]]. Climbing on top was your plan, but ice degrades climb performance, so a slow climb keeps you in the ice longer [[38:45|AC 91-74B 5-4a(2)]] [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(7)]]. Get out the surest way: leave the cloud and precipitation, or go to an altitude where it is above freezing. Here that means descending below the 4,000 ft freezing level, terrain and MEAs permitting [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]] [[38:46|AC 91-74B 5-4a(3)]].

questions.q: The controller is too busy to give you a clearance. What do you do?
questions.a: Declare an emergency and exit the icing as soon as practical, telling ATC what you are doing [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b(1)]] [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b]]. Pilots who deviated without declaring have ended up in conflict with ATC [[38:10|AC 91-74B 1-4b]].

questions.q: Which systems do you check or turn on right away?
questions.a: Pitot heat on and confirm the airspeed is believable [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-6a]], defroster on high [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-5d]], and carb heat or alternate air if power drops [[24:258|AFH 13-9]]. Be ready to use the alternate static source if the altimeter or VSI freeze [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

questions.q: You get below the freezing level with some ice still on the airplane. How do you fly the approach and landing?
questions.a: No AFM icing speed, so approach at least 25% faster and expect much longer landing distance; choose a longer runway [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10f]]. Consider a reduced-flap landing [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10f]]. Add flaps in stages and watch how the airplane behaves at each one. If it acts oddly, stop adding flaps and follow the maker's guidance on retracting them [[38:50|AC 91-74B 5-10a]] [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10a(2)]]. Carry power and limit the flare [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-10g]].

questions.q: What should you report after you are safe?
questions.a: File a PIREP with the icing type, intensity, altitude, aircraft type and OAT [[34:104|AIM 7-1-19]]. Under IFR in controlled airspace, unforecast weather must be reported [[60:482|14 CFR 91.183(b)]].

skills.do: Using the POH/AFM for the airplane on the test, show whether it is approved for flight in icing, name its ice protection (pitot and static heat, carb heat or alternate air, defroster, any boots or fluid system), explain how and when to use each, and state its limitations.
skills.practice: Find the icing approval in the AFM or TCDS using the AC 91-74B 3-12c clues [[38:31|AC 91-74B 3-12c]]. Walk the IFH instrument preflight and the AC 91-74B small-airplane icing checklist on your airplane [[23:132|IFH 5-37]] [[38:59|AC 91-74B App 2]].

skills.do: If the airplane has an autopilot, explain its modes, how to engage and disconnect it, its limitations, and what to do if it fails, using the AFM supplement.
skills.practice: In flight with your instructor, call out engaged and armed modes after every change, practice the disconnect, and hand-fly the same segment [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]] [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]]. Brief before each flight how you will handle an autopilot failure [[1:66|PHAK 2-27]].

quiz.q: Which statement describes a deicing system rather than an anti-icing system?
options: It is turned on before entering icing to keep the surface clean
It must run continuously from engine start to shutdown
It is used after ice forms and lets some ice build between cycles
It only protects the pitot tube and static ports
quiz.why: Deicing systems are activated after encountering icing and permit some accumulation [[38:23|AC 91-74B 3-4]]. Anti-icing is turned on beforehand to keep the surface free [[38:25|AC 91-74B 3-5]].

quiz.q: Unless the AFM says otherwise, when does the FAA recommend you first cycle pneumatic boots?
options: After 1/4 inch of ice builds
After 1/2 inch, to avoid ice bridging
At the first indication of icing
Only on the approach
quiz.why: Activating early and often never leaves more ice on the wing than waiting [[38:24|AC 91-74B 3-4a(2)]]. Bridging has few, if any, documented cases on modern boots [[38:24|AC 91-74B 3-4a(4)]].

quiz.q: Ice blocks the pitot tube opening but the drain hole stays open. What does the airspeed indicator do?
options: Slowly drops to zero
Acts like an altimeter
Freezes at the current reading
Reads high in the descent
quiz.why: Static pressure equalizes on both sides of the diaphragm and the indicated airspeed slowly drops to zero [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]. It acts like an altimeter only if the drain hole is also blocked.

quiz.q: You select a cabin alternate static source. What do you expect?
options: Altimeter slightly high, airspeed high, brief climb on the VSI
Altimeter slightly low, airspeed low, brief descent on the VSI
No change in any instrument
Altimeter frozen and VSI at zero
quiz.why: Cabin pressure is lower than outside, so the altimeter reads slightly higher, the ASI reads greater than actual, and the VSI shows a momentary climb [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

quiz.q: Your airplane is certificated for IFR. What does that tell you about flight in icing conditions?
options: It is approved for light icing only
Nothing by itself; check the AFM or POH
It is approved if pitot heat works
It is approved for known icing
quiz.why: An aircraft certificated for IFR is not necessarily certificated for flight in icing conditions; the AFM or POH must be consulted [[38:10|AC 91-74B 1-4a]].

quiz.q: After flying in ice, you lower flaps and feel elevator pulsing and a nose-down pitch. Best first action?
options: Engage the autopilot so it holds attitude while the pulsing passes
Add full power and lower the nose to gain speed before the next step
Extend full flaps to lower the stall speed and restore elevator feel
Retract flaps to the previous setting and apply nose-up elevator
quiz.why: These are tailplane stall signs. Retract flaps to the previous setting and apply nose-up elevator. Extra speed at the same flap setting makes a tail stall worse, so diving for speed is the wrong fix [[23:93|IFH 4-16]].

quiz.q: In a glass-panel airplane the alternator fails in IMC. How does the IFH treat this?
options: As a minor abnormal; continue to the destination and monitor the battery
As a reason to switch off the standby battery to save its charge
As normal; the standby battery will power the panel for the whole flight
As an emergency; shed load and land as soon as practical
quiz.why: In technically advanced aircraft, alternator failure is considered an emergency. Reduce the load and land as soon as practical [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

quiz.q: In icing, why is climbing with the autopilot in vertical speed mode discouraged?
options: VS mode turns off the pitot heat once a climb rate is selected
The autopilot holds the rate as ice builds, until the stall
VS mode cannot level off at the assigned altitude in icing conditions
It disables the boots and the heated windshield while it is engaged
quiz.why: Ice reduces climb performance; if the vertical speed is not reduced, the autopilot keeps the rate until stall [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-6d]].

quiz.q: With some autopilots in NAV mode, you switch the CDI source from GPS to LOC. What may happen?
options: The autopilot captures the localizer by itself once the source changes
NAV mode drops and the autopilot goes to ROL (wings level)
The autopilot disconnects and sounds the warning horn at once
Nothing happens; the autopilot ignores a source change made in NAV mode
quiz.why: Changing the navigation source while in NAV mode can make NAV disengage, with lateral control defaulting to ROL until you reengage it [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

quiz.q: Which parts make up the primary flight controls?
options: Ailerons, elevator (or stabilator) and rudder
Flaps, slats and spoilers
Trim tabs and the autopilot servos
Ailerons, flaps and trim
quiz.why: Ailerons, elevator or stabilator, and rudder are the primary system; flaps, leading edge devices, spoilers and trim are secondary [[1:150|PHAK 6-2]].

takeaways: IFR approval is not icing approval. The AFM and its limits (91.9) decide.
Anti-ice before you enter; deice at the first sign of ice. Neither lets you stay in ice indefinitely.
Pitot heat on before cloud. Know each blockage picture and when to use alternate static.
Ice cuts lift and raises stall speed. Keep 1.5 to 1.6 × Vs and fly the approach faster.
Tail stall comes with flaps; go back to the last flap setting. Wing stall: lower the angle of attack.
Vacuum or alternator failure: cross-check, use what works, shed load, tell ATC, land soon.
Autopilots hide ice and hold altitude or VS into a stall. Know the modes and watch airspeed.
cfi_notes: The IFH icing intensity list (11-2) is outdated: it says trace needs no equipment unless over 1 hour and light is no problem with equipment on. Teach the current AIM 7-1-19 definitions, which say to consider exiting even trace and light [[23:327|IFH 11-2]] [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]].
IFH 4-17 sends readers to AC 91-51, which AC 91-74B canceled (as AC 91-51A). Use AC 91-74B as the current icing guide [[23:94|IFH 4-17]] [[38:5|AC 91-74B 1-2]].

Students often quote 14 CFR 91.527 for their trainer. It is subpart F (large and turbojet multiengine airplanes). Have them find the icing limitation in their own AFM and tie it to 91.9 [[60:527|14 CFR 91.501(a)]] [[38:43|AC 91-74B 5-2]].

The IFH says an iced tail may stall after full or partial flaps; AC 91-74B says no ICTS is known with partial flaps. Teach that it is most likely at full flaps but stay alert at any flap change [[23:92|IFH 4-15]] [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-12a]].

Examiners commonly ask: is this airplane approved for icing and how do you know, what does each blockage look like, where is the alternate static and what does it do, and how is the autopilot disconnected.
Many AC 91-74B and IFH examples (PA-34, bleed air, EPR probes) come from twins and turbines. Use them only for the idea, and keep the student on the single-engine airplane they will fly.

Cover the attitude and heading indicators often in training so vacuum failure becomes routine; insist the student finds the OFF flags and the suction gauge first [[23:332|IFH 11-7]] [[23:333|IFH 11-8]].

Battery times differ by source (about 40 minutes in IFH 11-5, maybe 45 minutes or only minutes in 11-6, amp-hour math in AFH 18-13). Teach that the number is unknown, so shed load and land [[23:330|IFH 11-5]] [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].
gaps: The ice protection procedures, kinds-of-operations limits and autopilot limitations (S1, S2) of the specific airplane come from its POH/AFM and supplements, which are not in these sources.
No source here gives operating details for specific GA systems such as fluid (weeping wing) panels, heated prop timers or a named autopilot model beyond general descriptions.
AC 91-51A, AC 23.143-1 and AC 135-17, cited by the IFH and AC 91-74B, are not uploaded; tailplane stall and small airplane ground deicing are taught from AC 91-74B and the IFH only.
Multiengine items (dual pumps and check valves, alternator paralleling, engine-out climb with bleed air) and turbine-only items (EPR probes, ice crystal engine icing) are left out or only mentioned.
Some in-flight weather services named in AC 91-74B 5-3 may be out of date; this lesson does not teach them. Use the AIM for current services.

activities.title: Anti-ice or deice?
activities.intro: Tap a clue, then tap where it belongs.

items.t: Chemical fluid weeping from wing panels
Leading-edge heat cycled on and off to shed ice

activities.title: Read the pitot-static picture
activities.intro: Tap a failure, then the indication it causes.

pairs.r: Airspeed rises in a climb like an altimeter
Altimeter freezes and VSI stays at zero
Brief VSI climb, then altitude a bit high
Too high, too fast, descent rate too low

activities.title: Handle a gyro failure in IMC
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Keep control of the airplane and speed up your cross-check
Compare the attitude indicator with the turn indicator and VSI
Identify the failed instruments and fly on the ones that work
Try to restore them: check the power source, switch to backup, reset
Advise ATC and declare an emergency if needed

activities.title: Read the autopilot display
activities.intro: Each pin sits right beside one item on the autopilot display. Drag each name to its numbered pin.
activities.why: The display shows which modes are engaged and which are armed, and you must know both and check that armed modes engage on time [[24:257|AFH 13-8]] [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]]. HDG is heading mode [[23:119|IFH 5-24]]: a roll mode, the way LOC tracking is a roll mode, while vertical speed (V/S) is a pitch mode for climbing or descending [[29:176|IPH 4-36]]. VS HLD is vertical speed hold [[1:160|PHAK 6-12]], and VS400 with the up arrow is the vertical speed the pilot set, a 400 fpm climb [[29:176|IPH 4-36]]. APR ARM is the approach mode armed, waiting to capture [[1:70|PHAK 2-31]].

activities.title: True or false: flying in ice
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: An airplane approved for flight in known icing is also approved for freezing drizzle and freezing rain.
cards.why: No. Icing certification does not include freezing drizzle or freezing rain, and some airplanes are prohibited from them [[38:43|AC 91-74B 5-2a]].

cards.s: With ice on the wing, it stalls at a lower angle of attack and a higher airspeed.
cards.why: Yes. An iced wing ordinarily stalls at a lower AOA and thus a higher airspeed [[38:52|AC 91-74B 5-11a]].

cards.s: If there are no recent icing PIREPs on your route, there is no ice there.
cards.why: No. Maybe nobody flew there, or they didn't report it. Icing varies a lot in space and time [[38:40|AC 91-74B 4-3]].

cards.s: The warmer altitude that gets you out of ice is always a lower altitude.
cards.why: No. The warmer altitude may not always be lower [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]].

cards.s: Cycle the boots before beginning the approach, because it is better not to use them while landing.
cards.why: Yes. Boot use may increase stall speed, so cycle them before the approach [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10a(3)]].

cards.s: If you can no longer hold airspeed by adding power in ice, you should exit the icing conditions immediately.
cards.why: Yes. AC 91-74B says to exit immediately at that point [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-7b]].

activities.title: Ice in the clouds at 9,000 feet
activities.intro: You are flying N123AB, a single-engine piston airplane approved for flight in known icing, with deice boots, an electrically heated (deice) prop, windshield anti-ice and pitot heat, but no autothrottle. You are IFR at 9,000 ft in solid cloud with the autopilot in altitude hold. Clean stall speed (Vs) is 62 knots, and the AFM gives no icing airspeed.

steps.s: The OAT drops from +4 °C to +1 °C. You are in cloud, but no ice has formed yet.
options: Wait until you see ice, then turn on all the systems
Turn on windshield anti-ice now and confirm pitot heat is on
Inflate the boots now and keep cycling them every minute
Select the alternate static source as a precaution
steps.why: Anti-ice systems prevent ice, so turn them on at the first sign of visible moisture when the temperature is a little above freezing. Deice systems, like boots and the heated prop, are for ice that has already formed [[38:59|AC 91-74B App 2]] [[38:24|AC 91-74B 3-4c]]. Pitot heat should already be on from takeoff into cloud [[38:47|AC 91-74B 5-6a]].

steps.s: Rime now builds on the leading edges and the boots are shedding it. Workload is low, and the autopilot is still holding altitude.
options: Leave the autopilot on at all times, since it will trim out the ice effects
Reduce power to hold a lower angle of attack and lessen the ice buildup
Disengage the autopilot now and then and hand-fly to feel the handling
Switch to vertical speed mode for a smoother ride in the ice
steps.why: If workload permits, periodically disengage the autopilot and fly by hand to find handling changes caused by ice. The autopilot can mask them [[38:60|AC 91-74B App 2]] [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7e]].

steps.s: Center asks you to slow to 90 knots for spacing.
options: Tell ATC you are in ice and unable; you need about 93 to 99 knots
Accept, because 90 knots is well above the 62-knot clean stall speed
Accept and lower some flaps to give yourself extra stall margin
Accept and add power only if the stall horn sounds as ice builds
steps.why: With no AFM icing speed, keep at least 50% to 60% above Vs: 62 x 1.5 = 93 and 62 x 1.6 = 99.2 knots. Do not accept an ATC speed below that margin [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-7a]] [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b(3)]].

steps.s: The boots now need frequent cycling, and about an inch of ice builds on the unprotected outer wing every 30 minutes.
options: Stay at 9,000 ft, since the airplane is approved for icing and the boots are working
Climb at full power in vertical speed mode to find the tops above the ice
Start down 2,000 ft right away without telling ATC, since the ice is moderate
Report moderate icing and its effects, and ask ATC for a new route or altitude
steps.why: An inch per 30 minutes is 2 inches per hour with frequent boot cycling: moderate icing, so consider exiting as soon as possible [[34:103|AIM 7-1-19]]. Tell ATC how bad it is, what it is doing to the airplane, and what change you need [[38:44|AC 91-74B 5-2b]] [[23:327|IFH 11-2]].

steps.s: ATC says the freezing level is below the MEA, and the reported tops are far above you. An airport with an ILS and a long runway is 15 miles away. Your destination is 70 miles ahead.
options: Continue to the destination; the ice protection can handle it
Ask for a climb toward the tops at best rate
Ask to hold where you are until the ice sheds
Divert and land at the nearby airport
steps.why: If you cannot leave the precipitation or reach above-freezing air, consider landing at the nearest suitable airport. Ice protection gives you time to get out; it does not let you stay in ice indefinitely [[23:327|IFH 11-2]]. Holding is slower, so you collect more ice [[38:50|AC 91-74B 5-9a]].

final_quiz.q: Your clean stall speed (Vs) is 64 knots and the AFM gives no icing speed. Using AC 91-74B, what is the minimum airspeed to keep in icing conditions?
options: About 96 to 102 knots, or 50% to 60% above Vs
About 77 knots, which is 20% above the clean stall speed
About 80 knots, which is 25% above the clean stall speed
About 128 knots, which is double the clean stall speed
final_quiz.why: Maintain at least 50% to 60% above Vs clean: 64 × 1.5 = 96 and 64 × 1.6 = about 102 knots [[38:48|AC 91-74B 5-7a]].

final_quiz.q: You normally fly final at 80 knots. Ice remains on the airframe and the AFM has no icing approach speed. What final approach speed does AC 91-74B suggest at a minimum?
options: 85 knots, about 6% above the normal speed
90 knots, about 12% above the normal speed
100 knots, 25% above the normal speed
96 knots, 20% above the normal speed
final_quiz.why: Increase approach airspeed by at least 25% above the non-icing speed: 80 × 1.25 = 100 knots [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10f]].

final_quiz.q: Your normal landing distance is 1,400 ft. With ice, you fly the approach 20% faster. Using the AC 91-74B estimate, about how much landing distance should you expect?
options: 1,680 ft, about 20% more than normal
1,960 ft, about 40% more than normal
1,820 ft, about 30% more than normal
2,800 ft, about double the normal distance
final_quiz.why: Landing distance grows about 20% for each 10% more speed. 20% faster gives about 40% more: 1,400 × 1.4 = 1,960 ft [[38:51|AC 91-74B 5-10f]]. 1,680 ft is the 10% case.

final_quiz.q: Your alternator fails and the 25 amp-hour battery is carrying a 40-amp load. According to the AFH, about how long might the battery last?
options: About 5 hours, because a 25 amp-hour battery lasts that long
About 40 minutes, with the full rated capacity available
About 2 hours, if you shed only the non-essential lights
About 10 or 15 minutes
final_quiz.why: The AFH says a 40-amp load might discharge the battery fully in about 10 or 15 minutes [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. That is why you shed load right away.

final_quiz.q: You fly a single-engine piston airplane under Part 91. Which rule makes its "no flight into known icing" placard legally binding?
final_quiz.why: 91.527 is in subpart F, which applies to large and turbojet multiengine airplanes. For other GA aircraft, 91.9 prohibits flying outside the AFM limitations and placards [[38:43|AC 91-74B 5-2]] [[60:436|14 CFR 91.9(a)]].

final_quiz.q: You are checking a used airplane with boots on the wings. Which clue shows it is certificated for flight in icing?
options: The boots and a heated windshield are installed on the airplane
The airplane is approved for IFR flight and has pitot heat
The POH refers to part 25 appendix C icing conditions
The POH has only a list of the icing equipment installed
final_quiz.why: A reference to part 25 appendix C or 23.1419 at Amendment 23-14 or later shows icing certification. Only an equipment list means an older basis [[38:31|AC 91-74B 3-12c]]. Equipment alone does not mean approval [[24:258|AFH 13-9]].

final_quiz.q: In cruise at OAT +2 °C in drizzle, you notice jagged ice behind the boots and granular ice on the side windows. What is this telling you?
options: Normal rime ice; keep cycling the boots and stay at altitude
Possible SLD; request a route or altitude change to exit
Carburetor ice; apply full carb heat and enrich the mixture
Frost from cold-soaked fuel; it will sublimate as you climb
final_quiz.why: Ice aft of protected areas and granular ice on side windows are SLD cues, especially with drizzle below +5 °C. Request a change to exit [[38:34|AC 91-74B 3-16]].

final_quiz.q: In a descent the altimeter shows you too high, airspeed too fast, and the VSI shows a slow descent. A climb then makes airspeed drop alarmingly. What is the best way to confirm the problem?
options: Turn the pitot heat off and on to clear the blockage
Tap the instrument panel to free any sticking instruments
Open the alternate static source while climbing or descending
Reset the altimeter to 29.92 and compare it to the GPS altitude
final_quiz.why: That is a partial static blockage. Open the alternate static while climbing or descending; if the needles move a lot, use it for the rest of the flight [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

final_quiz.q: In IMC, the attitude indicator shows a slow left roll. The turn coordinator shows wings level, and altitude and VSI are steady. What should you do first?
options: Roll right until the attitude indicator shows level, then trim to hold that attitude
Climb to get above the clouds and back into visual conditions first
Engage the autopilot to level the wings and watch the attitude indicator
Trust the turn coordinator and static instruments; check suction and flags
final_quiz.why: Compare the attitude indicator with the rate-of-turn indicator and VSI, identify the failure, and use the working instruments. Vacuum gyros wander as they slow and can mislead the autopilot too [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

final_quiz.q: You are level in ice with the autopilot in altitude hold and no autothrottle. What should you watch most closely?
options: Airspeed, because the autopilot will hold altitude as speed decays
Heading, because ice makes the autopilot turn
The VSI, because altitude hold climbs in ice
Oil temperature, because ice blocks cooling
final_quiz.why: As ice accretes without autothrottles, the autopilot holds altitude without regard for airspeed, leading toward a stall [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7f]].

final_quiz.q: After 30 minutes on the autopilot in ice, you disconnect it for the approach. What should you be ready for?
options: No change, since the autopilot was trimming normally the whole time
An automatic flap extension as the system reverts to approach mode
Unusual control forces or a sudden control deflection
Loss of pitot heat when the autopilot servos are released
final_quiz.why: The autopilot can mask icing effects; at disconnect you may need extra force, and on unboosted controls it can disconnect with the controls deflected [[38:49|AC 91-74B 5-7e]].

final_quiz.q: Your up-elevator cable breaks in flight. The down cable still works. How can you keep pitch control?
options: Use lots of nose-down trim, then use back pressure to hold the nose up
Lower full flaps and reduce power to keep the nose from dropping
Engage the autopilot pitch hold to take over the pitch control
Use lots of nose-up trim, then forward pressure to control pitch
final_quiz.why: With a lost up-elevator cable, apply considerable nose-up trim and push forward to hold the attitude; relax forward pressure to raise the nose [[24:360|AFH 18-11]].

final_quiz.q: Flying a fixed-pitch prop in cloud near freezing, the rpm slowly drops. You apply full carburetor heat and the rpm drops further, then slowly rises. What happened?
options: The carburetor heat failed and the engine is losing power
The propeller is icing and then shedding its ice
The alternate static source opened and changed the airflow
Carburetor ice was present and is melting
final_quiz.why: With ice present and carb heat on, rpm drops and then gradually rises as the ice melts. Without ice, it drops and stays steady [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

final_quiz.q: In a glass-panel airplane the standby battery switch was left OFF and the alternator fails. Why does this matter?
options: The standby battery will drain the main battery faster than normal
It won't power the essential bus once the main battery runs down
The PFD will switch to a reversionary mode and keep working
Nothing; the standby battery comes on by itself when needed
final_quiz.why: The standby battery comes online near 19 volts only if its switch is in ARM. Arm it before departure [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].
